title: Kidney Stones: No! Please, NO!
summary: Josh and Chuck promote their upcoming live show at the SF Sketchfest in San Francisco, then discuss kidney stones: how common they are, where they form in the urinary tract, compositions (calcium oxalate, struvite, uric acid, cystine, xanthine), causes and diet, symptoms and renal colic pain, treatments from passing stones and medication to lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, and surgery, prevention through hydration and diet, how stones are passed, and a brief history from ancient times to Celsus and the lithotomy. The episode closes with listener mail from Tony in the UK about the origin of the "toothworm" phrase.

segments.title: SF Sketchfest live show promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote their live show at SF Sketchfest on January 1 at the Sydney Goldstein Theater in San Francisco, with vaccination proof required.

segments.title: Opening banter about kidney stones
segments.summary: Hosts open by asking whether either has had a kidney stone, note the roughly ten percent lifetime risk, and mention that kidney stone complications kill many people each year.

segments.title: Locations of kidney stones in the urinary tract
segments.summary: The hosts describe the urinary tract, including kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra, and explain that stones are classified by location; upper tract stones tend to be more serious and tiny stones can pass unnoticed.

segments.title: Kidney stone composition
segments.summary: Stones form when minerals precipitate out of urine and attract more material. The main types are calcium oxalate (most common), struvite (infection stones linked to alkaline urine and bacteria), uric acid (linked to gout and purines), cystine (rare, congenital), and xanthine (rare, linked to purines in caffeine).

segments.title: How stones form and their shapes
segments.summary: Stones grow as crystals around nodes such as renal papillae, compared to snowflakes, and can detach and float. Nicknames like stag horn, widow maker, and Judas Priest are mentioned, along with comparisons of smooth versus spiky stones.

segments.title: Symptoms, nerves, and pain
segments.summary: Symptoms often begin as lower back, side, or groin pain. The renal hilum houses nerves that cause nausea and referred pain. Kidney stone pain is described as among the worst, coming in renal colic waves, with the hosts exchanging anecdotes and a brief digression on documentaries and music.

segments.title: Treatment options: passing, medication, and lithotripsy
segments.summary: Small stones may be passed with fluids, pain medication, and tamsulosin-type relief. Imaging and urine and blood tests identify the stone. Larger stones may need extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy, which uses ultrasound to break them up.

segments.title: Ureteroscopy and percutaneous nephrolithotomy
segments.summary: Ureteroscopy uses a scope through the urethra to capture or laser-break stones, sometimes followed by a stent. For very large stones, percutaneous nephrolithotomy removes them through a small incision in the lower back. The record stone from India in 2004 was about five inches in diameter.

segments.title: Preventing kidney stones
segments.summary: Primary prevention centers on drinking plenty of water, which a study linked to fewer stones, and limiting animal protein, salt, and oxalate-rich foods like spinach and chocolate, without cutting calcium too much. Secondary prevention for chronic stone formers includes medication and monitoring urine pH.

segments.title: How stones are passed and the pain stages
segments.summary: Stones cause pain when they detach. Spasms push the stone along, with the urethra being narrow. A stone can get stuck and become a bladder stone; the hosts advise pushing repeatedly until it passes.

segments.title: History of kidney stone treatment
segments.summary: Kidney stones have existed since ancient times, with a mummy showing evidence. Celsus, around 50 CE, described surgical lithotomy through the perineum. Mortality from lithotomy remained near a quarter of patients into the nineteenth century.

segments.title: Listener mail: toothworms
segments.summary: Listener Tony, a dental nurse from London, suggests the Babylonian toothworm idea may come from the look of an exposed tooth nerve. Chuck shares that a tooth nerve he had removed looked like a small white worm.
